comment: What a settlement sounds like. Templates keyed by (belief band x speaker), with each myth slotting its own nouns in. 16 buckets, ~5 lines each: structural coverage so no myth is ever silent, with bespoke lines authored per myth on top. Children are the leading indicator - they learn what is common, so their voices dry up a band ahead of everyone else, and a myth no child mentions is one generation from gone.

child: We were playing {subject} down by {place} all afternoon.
Don't say it three times near {place}. Everyone knows that.
My brother can do the whole rhyme. All of it.
That's not how it goes, you've got the verse wrong.
worker: Wouldn't go near {place} after dark. Not this month.
Left something out for {subject} before we started. You should too.
Saw {sign} on the way in. Made me walk the long way round.
My mother did it the same way, and hers before that.
elder: I've told it the same way sixty years and I'll not change it now.
There's nine verses. Most only know the first three.
{sign}. That's the old sign, and people still know it.
My grandmother heard it from someone who saw it.
You want the full telling, come back when I've had my supper.
priest: We keep the marker at {place}. It's maintained.
The telling is this month. The whole village comes.
It is not superstition. It is an account of what happened.
I have the verses written. All nine of them.
We observe it properly here, whatever they do downriver.

child: I think there's a song about {subject}? My gran sings it.
Is {sign} real? Davey says it's real.
We don't play that one much any more.
My mum says not to talk about it at the table.
worker: Oh aye, {subject}. Haven't thought about that in a while.
There's a thing about {place}, isn't there.
My father used to say {verb}. Never knew if he meant it.
I'd know the tune if you hummed it.
People still leave things out. Some people.
elder: They don't tell it right any more. But they tell it.
I know six verses. There were nine.
Ask anyone over fifty. The young ones, less so.
{sign}. You'd not hear that mentioned now.
It'll last my lifetime. After that, who knows.
priest: The marker's still at {place}. Wants work.
We observe it. Attendance is what it is.
I have most of the verses. Not all of them.
It comes up at funerals, mostly, now.
People remember it when they need it.

child: My gran said something but I wasn't listening.
We don't have a song for that one.
worker: {subject}. That's an old one. Not sure anyone still tells it.
Something at {place}, years back. Couldn't tell you what.
You'd want to ask one of the old ones.
elder: I'm one of the last who has it whole, I think.
Nobody's asked me about that in years.
Three verses left in me. There were nine.
My sister knew it too. She's gone now.
Sit down, then. Someone ought to have it.
priest: The marker at {place} is overgrown. I should see to it.
We've not observed it properly in some time.
I have it written somewhere. I'd have to look.
It's in the book. Nobody reads the book.
There's no one left who would come.

worker: Is that a real one, or did you make it up?
elder: I know the second verse. Only the second. I don't know why that one stayed.
There was a name for it. It's gone out of me.
My mother had it. I let it go.
If you've got any of it, write it down. Don't do what I did.
You're the first to ask in thirty years.
priest: There's a line in the book I can't account for. It may be this.
The marker's gone. Taken for a wall, probably.
I couldn't tell you the first verse. I'm sorry.

markers.thriving: The marker at {place} is swept, and something fresh has been left on it.
markers.ordinary: The marker at {place} is upright. Someone has been, though not lately.
markers.fading: The marker at {place} is under weeds. The carving is hard to make out.
markers.nearly_gone: There is a stone at {place}. Nothing on it you could call a carving.

land.fire: The rock is warm where it has no business being warm.
land.water: The low ground is holding water that should have drained a week ago.
land.hunger: The barley is coming up thin and pale on the south side.
land.stone: There is more scree on the path than there was, and it is sharp.
land.growth: The hedges have gone over the walls, and nobody can keep up with them.
land.dusk: It gets dark earlier here than it ought to, and stays dark.

comment_bands: Band cuts are MULTIPLES of an even share (1/n for a region holding n myths), not absolute shares. Absolute cuts do not scale: a myth at 0.10 is thriving in a region of twenty stories and nearly dead in a region of three. Same scaling bug as per-myth decay.
